# Greenhouse effect, global warming, climate change

## 1. Introduction
Opening frame for **Greenhouse effect** — what the topic is, why it matters, a real-world hook (Nepal where possible), the map of what follows, and the learning outcomes (biology-plan.md §3.1, block I). Prose depth is written in the Environmental Issues fill pass.

## 2. Hierarchy body — every syllabus sub-point
### Greenhouse effect
### global warming
### climate change

Fill order per concept: definition → structure → process → significance (§3.2). Step-by-step numbered points, Pioneer style.

The **greenhouse effect** is natural and life-giving: CO2, CH4, water vapour and other gases let sunlight in but slow the infrared escape, keeping Earth ~33°C warmer than it would be. The problem is the **enhanced** effect: fossil fuel burning and deforestation have raised CO2 from ~280 to over 420 ppm, driving **global warming** and with it **climate change** — shifting rainfall, melting ice, rising seas.

**Concept flow — from physics to politics (study in this order)**

| Step | Concept | Key fact |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Natural greenhouse effect | Shortwave in, longwave (IR) partially trapped — Earth would be −18°C without it |
| 2 | Enhanced effect | More CO2/CH4 → more IR trapped → surface warms |
| 3 | Main human causes | Fossil fuels, deforestation, cement, agriculture (CH4, N2O) |
| 4 | Observed warming | ~1.1–1.2°C above pre-industrial average |
| 5 | Consequences | Ice melt, sea-level rise, extreme weather, coral bleaching, shifting crop zones |
| 6 | Mitigation | Cut emissions: renewables, efficiency, afforestation, carbon pricing |
| 7 | Adaptation | Adjust to what is locked in: flood defences, drought-tolerant crops |

**The major greenhouse gases**

| Gas | Main human source | Notable point |
|---|---|---|
| CO2 | Fossil-fuel burning, deforestation, cement | Largest contributor by volume — the benchmark gas |
| CH4 (methane) | Livestock, rice paddies, landfills, gas leaks | Far stronger than CO2 per molecule (~25× over a century) |
| N2O | Nitrogen fertilisers, combustion | Also damages the ozone layer |
| CFCs (now phased down) | Old refrigerants and aerosols | Banned by the Montreal Protocol — also ozone destroyers |
| Water vapour | Evaporation (natural) | Most abundant greenhouse gas — a feedback, not a primary driver |

**Mitigation vs adaptation — the two responses**

| Response | Meaning | Examples |
|---|---|---|
| Mitigation | Reduce the cause — cut emissions | Solar and wind power, energy-efficient buildings, afforestation, electric transport, methane capture |
| Adaptation | Reduce the harm — adjust to change | Flood embankments, drought-tolerant crop varieties, early-warning systems, water storage |
| International frameworks | Shared targets | Kyoto Protocol (1997, binding targets), Paris Agreement (2015, well below 2°C, efforts toward 1.5°C) |

## 6. Key terms and statements
Every new term defined once; exam-grade definitions live here and in keyPoints (block VI).

**Worked example — why methane cuts pay fast.** CO2 persists for centuries, so its warming is slow to reverse. Methane's lifetime is only ~12 years. Cutting methane leaks (landfills, gas systems, livestock feed additives) therefore slows near-term warming within a decade — the fastest lever available while the slow CO2 transition proceeds. Two gases, two time-scales, one strategy.

examShortTricks: Trick 1: Mechanism: greenhouse gases (CO2, CH4, N2O, CFCs) transmit incoming short-wave sunlight but absorb outgoing long-wave infrared → warming — the one-way valve picture.
Trick 2: Gas potency: CH4 ~25× CO2 (20-yr), CFCs thousands× — quote one multiplier; CO2 dominates by volume.
Trick 3: Consequences: sea-level rise (thermal expansion + ice melt), extreme weather, coral bleaching, disease spread — four consequences.
Trick 4: Controls: Kyoto Protocol/Paris Agreement, afforestation, renewable energy, energy efficiency — the policy plus practice list.
